cards.definition: **Definition.** An ACL associates a resource with entries identifying principals and allowed or denied operations.
major_error_concepts: Checking an ACL entry without resolving inheritance, deny precedence, and current principal identity.
cards.prompt: Define access control list. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: An ACL associates a resource with entries identifying principals and allowed or denied operations.

cards.definition: **Definition.** An adversarial security-test input is generated or selected to exercise parser, state, resource, trust-boundary, and misuse behavior under an explicit threat hypothesis rather than only ordinary valid use.
major_error_concepts: Calling random malformed bytes adversarial without a target surface, generation model, or threat rationale.
cards.prompt: Define adversarial security-test input. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: An adversarial security-test input is generated or selected to exercise parser, state, resource, trust-boundary, and misuse behavior under an explicit threat hypothesis rather than only ordinary valid use.

cards.definition: **Definition.** An adversary model states attacker goals, knowledge, access, capabilities, resources, persistence, coordination, and constraints.
major_error_concepts: Describing an attacker as malicious without bounding what it can observe or do.
cards.prompt: Define adversary model. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: An adversary model states attacker goals, knowledge, access, capabilities, resources, persistence, coordination, and constraints.

cards.definition: **Definition.** An assurance case links security claims to arguments, assumptions, tests, analyses, operational evidence, and residual risks.
major_error_concepts: Treating compliance certification alone as proof of all security claims.
cards.prompt: Define security assurance case. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: An assurance case links security claims to arguments, assumptions, tests, analyses, operational evidence, and residual risks.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The attack surface is the set of reachable interfaces, inputs, dependencies, privileges, identities, and physical or operational paths through which compromise may be attempted.
major_error_concepts: Counting only public network ports and ignoring identities, dependencies, and internal boundaries.
cards.prompt: Define attack surface. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The attack surface is the set of reachable interfaces, inputs, dependencies, privileges, identities, and physical or operational paths through which compromise may be attempted.

cards.definition: **Definition.** An attack vector is the path or mechanism an adversary uses to reach and exploit a target, including preconditions and delivery surface.
major_error_concepts: Naming the resulting impact as the attack vector.
cards.prompt: Define attack vector. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: An attack vector is the path or mechanism an adversary uses to reach and exploit a target, including preconditions and delivery surface.

cards.definition: **Definition.** ABAC evaluates policy over subject, resource, action, and environment attributes, enabling context-sensitive authorization.
major_error_concepts: Trusting caller-supplied attributes without an authoritative source and integrity protection.
cards.prompt: Define attribute-based access control. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: ABAC evaluates policy over subject, resource, action, and environment attributes, enabling context-sensitive authorization.

cards.definition: **Definition.** An audit log is a protected, time-ordered record of security-relevant events with principal, action, resource, result, context, and correlation identifiers sufficient for detection and investigation.
major_error_concepts: Logging sensitive payloads indiscriminately and calling greater volume better auditability.
cards.prompt: Define security audit log. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: An audit log is a protected, time-ordered record of security-relevant events with principal, action, resource, result, context, and correlation identifiers sufficient for detection and investigation.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Authenticated encryption protects message confidentiality and integrity together, normally binding additional unencrypted context and requiring nonce discipline.
major_error_concepts: Using unauthenticated encryption and assuming modified ciphertext will be rejected.
cards.prompt: Define authenticated encryption. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Authenticated encryption protects message confidentiality and integrity together, normally binding additional unencrypted context and requiring nonce discipline.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Authenticated key exchange binds the negotiated shared key to authenticated peer identities and the protocol transcript while stating forward-secrecy, replay, downgrade, and key-compromise limits.
major_error_concepts: Checking a certificate separately from a key exchange without binding both to the same transcript and peer.
cards.prompt: Define authenticated key exchange. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Authenticated key exchange binds the negotiated shared key to authenticated peer identities and the protocol transcript while stating forward-secrecy, replay, downgrade, and key-compromise limits.

cards.definition: **Definition.** An authentication factor is evidence from one of the canonical classes: something the claimant knows, possesses, or is; factor independence depends on distinct compromise paths, not merely on different labels or prompts.
major_error_concepts: Counting two passwords as independent factors.
cards.prompt: Define authentication factor. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: An authentication factor is evidence from one of the canonical classes: something the claimant knows, possesses, or is; factor independence depends on distinct compromise paths, not merely on different labels or prompts.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Authorization decides whether an authenticated or otherwise identified principal may perform an operation on a resource in the current context.
major_error_concepts: Using successful authentication as permission for every operation.
cards.prompt: Define authorization. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Authorization decides whether an authenticated or otherwise identified principal may perform an operation on a resource in the current context.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Availability means authorized users can obtain required service and resources within declared timing, capacity, and failure conditions.
major_error_concepts: Calling a service available because one health endpoint responds while critical operations fail.
cards.prompt: Define availability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Availability means authorized users can obtain required service and resources within declared timing, capacity, and failure conditions.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A behavioral biometric signal estimates identity from patterns such as typing, motion, or voice behavior and counts as independent evidence only when enrollment, spoof resistance, error rates, liveness, and compromise paths justify that claim.
major_error_concepts: Calling any behavior score a separate inherence factor without testing shared compromise and presentation attacks.
cards.prompt: What boundary or limitation does behavioral biometric signal impose?
required_concepts: A behavioral biometric signal estimates identity from patterns such as typing, motion, or voice behavior and counts as independent evidence only when enrollment, spoof resistance, error rates, liveness, and compromise paths justify that claim.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A buffer overflow writes beyond an allocated region, potentially corrupting adjacent data or control state when memory safety is not enforced.
major_error_concepts: Calling every out-of-bounds read a buffer overflow write.
cards.prompt: Define buffer overflow. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A buffer overflow writes beyond an allocated region, potentially corrupting adjacent data or control state when memory safety is not enforced.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Build provenance records source, dependencies, build steps, environment, builder identity, and artifact digest so a release can be traced and policy checked.
major_error_concepts: Signing an artifact without recording what source and process produced it.
cards.prompt: Define build provenance. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Build provenance records source, dependencies, build steps, environment, builder identity, and artifact digest so a release can be traced and policy checked.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A capability is an unforgeable, transferable or nontransferable token of authority naming a resource and permitted operations.
major_error_concepts: Treating an object identifier as a capability when possession does not itself authorize access.
cards.prompt: Define security capability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A capability is an unforgeable, transferable or nontransferable token of authority naming a resource and permitted operations.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A digital certificate binds a subject identity or authorization scope to a public key through an issuer signature, validity interval, extensions, constraints, and a trust-path policy.
major_error_concepts: Treating possession of any signed certificate as authorization for every name, use, or trust domain.
cards.prompt: Define certificate public-key binding. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A digital certificate binds a subject identity or authorization scope to a public key through an issuer signature, validity interval, extensions, constraints, and a trust-path policy.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Certificate validation verifies a trust chain, names or identities, time validity, key usage, constraints, and relevant revocation or policy requirements.
major_error_concepts: Checking only that a certificate is signed by some certificate authority.
cards.prompt: Define certificate validation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Certificate validation verifies a trust chain, names or identities, time validity, key usage, constraints, and relevant revocation or policy requirements.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Channel binding ties an application authentication or authorization exchange to the underlying secure channel, preventing credentials from being relayed across a different channel.
major_error_concepts: Using TLS and application login independently and assuming relay is impossible.
cards.prompt: Define channel binding. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Channel binding ties an application authentication or authorization exchange to the underlying secure channel, preventing credentials from being relayed across a different channel.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Collision resistance is the computational property that an adversary cannot feasibly find two distinct inputs with the same hash digest under the stated security parameter and attack model.
major_error_concepts: Defining collision resistance as absence of collisions, which is impossible for a finite digest space.
cards.prompt: Define collision resistance. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Collision resistance is the computational property that an adversary cannot feasibly find two distinct inputs with the same hash digest under the stated security parameter and attack model.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Command injection lets untrusted input alter shell or interpreter command structure, commonly through unsafe string construction or argument parsing.
major_error_concepts: Escaping one metacharacter and assuming all shell and encoding contexts are safe.
cards.prompt: Define command injection. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Command injection lets untrusted input alter shell or interpreter command structure, commonly through unsafe string construction or argument parsing.

cards.definition: **Role and limitations.** Complete mediation prevents alternate paths, stale grants, and unchecked reuse from bypassing policy, while exposing the performance and cache-coherence cost of repeated authorization.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting it as repeated authentication rather than authorization of each sensitive access.
cards.prompt: What is complete mediation used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: Complete mediation prevents alternate paths, stale grants, and unchecked reuse from bypassing policy, while exposing the performance and cache-coherence cost of repeated authorization.

cards.definition: **Design principle.** Every security-sensitive access must be checked against the principal's current authority at an enforcement point; cached decisions require invalidation semantics that preserve revocation and context changes.
major_error_concepts: Checking permission only when a session or file handle is first created and ignoring later revocation.
cards.prompt: State the complete mediation design principle or requirements and its intended scope.
required_concepts: Every security-sensitive access must be checked against the principal's current authority at an enforcement point; cached decisions require invalidation semantics that preserve revocation and context changes.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Confidentiality restricts information disclosure to authorized parties and permitted contexts.
major_error_concepts: Treating encryption at rest as complete confidentiality across access, use, logs, and endpoints.
cards.prompt: Define confidentiality. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Confidentiality restricts information disclosure to authorized parties and permitted contexts.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A confused deputy occurs when a more privileged component is induced to use its authority on behalf of an unprivileged requester without correctly binding the requester's authority and intent.
major_error_concepts: Classifying every privilege-escalation bug as a confused deputy without an authority-confusion intermediary.
cards.prompt: Define confused deputy problem. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A confused deputy occurs when a more privileged component is induced to use its authority on behalf of an unprivileged requester without correctly binding the requester's authority and intent.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A container isolates namespaces, resources, and files while sharing a host kernel; its strength depends on kernel enforcement, configuration, capabilities, mounts, and surrounding controls.
major_error_concepts: Treating a default container as equivalent to a separate hardened virtual machine.
cards.prompt: Define container security boundary. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A container isolates namespaces, resources, and files while sharing a host kernel; its strength depends on kernel enforcement, configuration, capabilities, mounts, and surrounding controls.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A contextual authentication signal is evidence such as location, device posture, network, or risk history used to adjust assurance or policy but not automatically an independent authentication-factor class.
major_error_concepts: Counting location as an independent factor when it is inferred from the same compromised device or channel.
cards.prompt: What boundary or limitation does contextual authentication signal impose?
required_concepts: A contextual authentication signal is evidence such as location, device posture, network, or risk history used to adjust assurance or policy but not automatically an independent authentication-factor class.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The credential lifecycle covers issuance, binding, storage, use, rotation, recovery, suspension, revocation, expiration, and audit.
major_error_concepts: Designing initial login while leaving lost, stolen, or departed-user credentials valid.
cards.prompt: Define credential lifecycle. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The credential lifecycle covers issuance, binding, storage, use, rotation, recovery, suspension, revocation, expiration, and audit.

cards.definition: In classic authenticated cross-site request forgery, an attacker induces a browser to send an unintended security-relevant request that a site accepts using the browser user session or other ambient credentials. The server mistakes that ambient authority for evidence of the user intended action. The attacker need not read the response; being able to read it does not make the forged action cease to be CSRF. Merely making a harmless cross-origin request is not enough.
major_error_concepts: Rejecting a forged authenticated action as CSRF solely because its response is also readable.
Labeling every harmless cross-origin request a CSRF attack.
cards.prompt: What is classic authenticated cross-site request forgery, and does its classification depend on whether the attacker can read the response?
required_concepts: An attacker induces an unintended security-relevant request accepted through browser ambient authentication/authority.
Reading the response is unnecessary, not prohibited; distinguish the attack from an innocuous cross-origin request.

cards.definition: **Definition.** XSS injects attacker-controlled script into an origin's execution context, allowing access and actions with that origin's browser authority.
major_error_concepts: Treating server-side command injection as XSS.
cards.prompt: Define cross-site scripting. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: XSS injects attacker-controlled script into an origin's execution context, allowing access and actions with that origin's browser authority.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A cryptographic design begins with a precise goal such as confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, nonrepudiation, or key agreement under an adversary model.
major_error_concepts: Selecting a cipher before defining the property and attacker.
cards.prompt: Define cryptographic security goal. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A cryptographic design begins with a precise goal such as confidentiality, integrity, authenticity, nonrepudiation, or key agreement under an adversary model.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A cryptographic hash function deterministically maps arbitrary-length input to a fixed-length digest and is selected with explicit collision, preimage, and domain-separation requirements rather than secrecy.
major_error_concepts: Treating an unkeyed hash as encryption or message authentication.
cards.prompt: Define cryptographic hash function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A cryptographic hash function deterministically maps arbitrary-length input to a fixed-length digest and is selected with explicit collision, preimage, and domain-separation requirements rather than secrecy.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Key agreement lets parties contribute protocol values and derive shared key material without sending the resulting key directly, under stated group, randomness, and adversary assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Calling unauthenticated key agreement protection against an active man-in-the-middle attacker.
cards.prompt: Define cryptographic key agreement. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Key agreement lets parties contribute protocol values and derive shared key material without sending the resulting key directly, under stated group, randomness, and adversary assumptions.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A cryptographic key is secret or controlled material selecting a primitive instance, with generation, purpose, scope, storage, usage, rotation, and destruction defined.
major_error_concepts: Storing a key beside encrypted data under identical access controls and calling the data protected from that compromise.
cards.prompt: Define cryptographic key. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A cryptographic key is secret or controlled material selecting a primitive instance, with generation, purpose, scope, storage, usage, rotation, and destruction defined.

cards.definition: **Role and limitations.** Defense in depth reduces residual risk and improves recovery when controls fail, but it retains an explicit account of common-mode failures, bypass paths, operational cost, and remaining impact.
major_error_concepts: Using many controls to avoid stating residual risk and recovery assumptions.
cards.prompt: What is defense in depth used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: Defense in depth reduces residual risk and improves recovery when controls fail, but it retains an explicit account of common-mode failures, bypass paths, operational cost, and remaining impact.

cards.definition: Defense in depth places multiple controls across prevention, detection, containment and recovery to reduce the chance or impact of one control failure. Analyze whether controls fail independently, share dependencies or permit bypass; multiple controls alone do not guarantee acceptable residual risk.
major_error_concepts: Counting correlated controls on one vulnerable component as independent layers.
Treating a defense-in-depth label as a theorem that unacceptable harm cannot occur.
cards.prompt: State the defense-in-depth design principle and its limitations.
required_concepts: Combine controls across prevention, detection, containment and recovery to limit single-control failure impact.
Analyze common-mode dependencies and bypasses; the design principle is not a proof of zero residual risk.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Delegation grants a principal bounded authority to act for another, with scope, audience, chain, duration, attenuation, and revocation defined.
major_error_concepts: Forwarding an unrestricted root credential and calling it delegation.
cards.prompt: Define authorization delegation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Delegation grants a principal bounded authority to act for another, with scope, audience, chain, duration, attenuation, and revocation defined.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Dependency risk includes vulnerabilities, malicious updates, compromised maintainers, namespace confusion, abandoned code, transitive exposure, and build-time execution.
major_error_concepts: Auditing only direct dependencies and ignoring transitive and build dependencies.
cards.prompt: Define software dependency risk. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Dependency risk includes vulnerabilities, malicious updates, compromised maintainers, namespace confusion, abandoned code, transitive exposure, and build-time execution.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A digital identity is a set of attributes and identifiers bound to a principal within a defined administrative domain and lifecycle.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a globally unique email address proves one persistent real-world person.
cards.prompt: Define digital identity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A digital identity is a set of attributes and identifiers bound to a principal within a defined administrative domain and lifecycle.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A digital signature is produced with a private signing key and verified with the corresponding public key to authenticate a message and signer-key relation under the signature scheme and key-binding assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Calling a signature proof that the signer identity, timestamp, intent, or key custody was valid without the corresponding evidence.
cards.prompt: Define digital signature. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A digital signature is produced with a private signing key and verified with the corresponding public key to authenticate a message and signer-key relation under the signature scheme and key-binding assumptions.

cards.definition: **Definition.** DAST probes a running application through exposed interfaces to find observable security failures under tested inputs and configurations.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting no findings as proof that untested paths and internal components are secure.
cards.prompt: Define dynamic application security testing. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: DAST probes a running application through exposed interfaces to find observable security failures under tested inputs and configurations.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Economy of mechanism keeps security-critical designs small and simple enough to understand, implement, and verify.
major_error_concepts: Removing defense layers merely to reduce line count.
cards.prompt: Define economy of mechanism. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Economy of mechanism keeps security-critical designs small and simple enough to understand, implement, and verify.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A fail-safe default denies access unless permission is explicitly granted and moves failures toward the safer declared state.
major_error_concepts: Assuming fail-closed is always safer when loss of availability can itself be hazardous.
cards.prompt: Define fail-safe default. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A fail-safe default denies access unless permission is explicitly granted and moves failures toward the safer declared state.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A false positive is an alert on activity that does not satisfy the detection's target incident definition, consuming investigation capacity and potentially causing harmful response.
major_error_concepts: Labeling difficult-to-investigate alerts false positives without determining ground truth.
cards.prompt: Define security alert false positive. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A false positive is an alert on activity that does not satisfy the detection's target incident definition, consuming investigation capacity and potentially causing harmful response.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A firewall policy permits or denies network flows based on addresses, ports, protocols, connection state, identity, or application context at an enforcement boundary.
major_error_concepts: Assuming allowed traffic is trustworthy after it passes the firewall.
cards.prompt: Define firewall policy. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A firewall policy permits or denies network flows based on addresses, ports, protocols, connection state, identity, or application context at an enforcement boundary.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Forward secrecy limits retrospective session decryption after long-term key compromise by deriving ephemeral session secrets not recoverable from the later-compromised key alone.
major_error_concepts: Claiming forward secrecy protects sessions whose ephemeral secrets were also logged or compromised.
cards.prompt: Define forward secrecy. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Forward secrecy limits retrospective session decryption after long-term key compromise by deriving ephemeral session secrets not recoverable from the later-compromised key alone.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Fuzzing generates or mutates inputs to exercise parser, state-machine, and boundary behavior while monitoring crashes, hangs, invariant violations, and sanitizer signals.
major_error_concepts: Generating random bytes without coverage, grammar, or failure oracles and assuming adequate fuzzing.
cards.prompt: Define security fuzz testing. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Fuzzing generates or mutates inputs to exercise parser, state-machine, and boundary behavior while monitoring crashes, hangs, invariant violations, and sanitizer signals.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Identification asserts an identity label; authentication verifies evidence that the claimant controls or possesses credentials bound to that identity.
major_error_concepts: Treating entry of a username as authentication.
cards.prompt: Distinguish identification versus authentication.
required_concepts: Identification asserts an identity label; authentication verifies evidence that the claimant controls or possesses credentials bound to that identity.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Containment limits ongoing harm and spread through isolation, credential revocation, traffic controls, feature shutdown, or temporary mitigations while preserving evidence and critical operations.
major_error_concepts: Erasing compromised systems immediately and destroying evidence before scope is known.
cards.prompt: Define incident containment. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Containment limits ongoing harm and spread through isolation, credential revocation, traffic controls, feature shutdown, or temporary mitigations while preserving evidence and critical operations.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Eradication removes attacker persistence, malicious artifacts, compromised credentials, vulnerable paths, and root causes after containment.
major_error_concepts: Restoring service from a still-compromised image and calling the attacker removed.
cards.prompt: Define incident eradication. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Eradication removes attacker persistence, malicious artifacts, compromised credentials, vulnerable paths, and root causes after containment.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Recovery restores services and trust from verified clean states, monitors for recurrence, rotates affected authority, and validates business and security invariants.
major_error_concepts: Declaring recovery when uptime returns but credentials, data integrity, and persistence have not been checked.
cards.prompt: Define incident recovery. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Recovery restores services and trust from verified clean states, monitors for recurrence, rotates affected authority, and validates business and security invariants.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A security incident is a confirmed or sufficiently credible violation or imminent threat to security policy requiring coordinated response.
major_error_concepts: Calling every blocked attack attempt a realized incident without the organization's declared threshold.
cards.prompt: Define security incident. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A security incident is a confirmed or sufficiently credible violation or imminent threat to security policy requiring coordinated response.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Injection occurs when untrusted data is interpreted as commands, queries, templates, paths, or code because structure and data are not safely separated.
major_error_concepts: Defining injection only as SQL syntax attacks.
cards.prompt: Define injection vulnerability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Injection occurs when untrusted data is interpreted as commands, queries, templates, paths, or code because structure and data are not safely separated.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Input validation checks that data satisfy an expected grammar, type, range, size, and semantic constraints at a trust boundary.
major_error_concepts: Using validation alone where context-specific output encoding or parameterization is required.
cards.prompt: Define input validation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Input validation checks that data satisfy an expected grammar, type, range, size, and semantic constraints at a trust boundary.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Integrity protects data, code, state, and decisions from unauthorized or undetected modification and preserves relevant origin and completeness.
major_error_concepts: Defining integrity only as absence of accidental corruption.
cards.prompt: Define security integrity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Integrity protects data, code, state, and decisions from unauthorized or undetected modification and preserves relevant origin and completeness.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A KDF derives one or more cryptographic keys from source key material using salt, context, and declared cost or extraction-expansion properties.
major_error_concepts: Using a fast general hash of a password as a password KDF without salt and work factor.
cards.prompt: Define key derivation function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A KDF derives one or more cryptographic keys from source key material using salt, context, and declared cost or extraction-expansion properties.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Key rotation replaces active keys according to age, exposure, cryptoperiod, or incident criteria while preserving controlled decryption, migration, and revocation of older keys.
major_error_concepts: Generating a new key while leaving all systems indefinitely accepting the compromised key.
cards.prompt: Define key rotation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Key rotation replaces active keys according to age, exposure, cryptoperiod, or incident criteria while preserving controlled decryption, migration, and revocation of older keys.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Least common mechanism minimizes shared components and state between users or trust domains to reduce covert channels, interference, and common compromise.
major_error_concepts: Duplicating every component without considering patchability and newly enlarged attack surface.
cards.prompt: Define least common mechanism. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Least common mechanism minimizes shared components and state between users or trust domains to reduce covert channels, interference, and common compromise.

cards.definition: **Role and limitations.** Least privilege limits blast radius and misuse after error or compromise; it reduces impact but does not prevent the principal itself from being compromised.
major_error_concepts: Presenting least privilege as a guarantee that compromise cannot occur.
cards.prompt: What is principle of least privilege used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: Least privilege limits blast radius and misuse after error or compromise; it reduces impact but does not prevent the principal itself from being compromised.

cards.definition: **Design principle.** Each principal should receive only the resource, operation, scope, duration, and delegation authority necessary for its current task, with revocation and renewal defined.
major_error_concepts: Granting broad permanent access because it is operationally convenient.
cards.prompt: State the principle of least privilege and its intended scope.
required_concepts: Each principal should receive only the resource, operation, scope, duration, and delegation authority necessary for its current task, with revocation and renewal defined.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Lessons learned reconstruct the timeline, control failures, organizational contributors, impact, response performance, and owned corrective actions without reducing analysis to individual blame.
major_error_concepts: Writing a narrative without tracked control changes and verification dates.
cards.prompt: Define security incident lessons learned. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Lessons learned reconstruct the timeline, control failures, organizational contributors, impact, response performance, and owned corrective actions without reducing analysis to individual blame.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A MAC uses one shared secret for tag creation and verification, whereas a digital signature separates private signing from public verification; their key ownership, verifier population, and attribution properties therefore differ.
major_error_concepts: Calling a shared-key MAC publicly verifiable or calling every signature nonrepudiation evidence.
cards.prompt: Distinguish MAC versus digital signature.
required_concepts: A MAC uses one shared secret for tag creation and verification, whereas a digital signature separates private signing from public verification; their key ownership, verifier population, and attribution properties therefore differ.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Memory safety prevents invalid reads, writes, frees, and type-confused memory access, reducing corruption and control-flow attacks but not logical authorization flaws.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a memory-safe language makes an application secure.
cards.prompt: Define memory safety. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Memory safety prevents invalid reads, writes, frees, and type-confused memory access, reducing corruption and control-flow attacks but not logical authorization flaws.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A message authentication code uses a shared secret key to produce and verify a tag that authenticates message integrity and origin to parties holding that key.
major_error_concepts: Using an unkeyed hash as a MAC or claiming a MAC proves which shared-key holder created a message.
cards.prompt: Define message authentication code. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A message authentication code uses a shared secret key to produce and verify a tag that authenticates message integrity and origin to parties holding that key.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A misuse case describes an adversarial or accidental sequence that violates a security objective, including actors, preconditions, path, impact, and candidate controls.
major_error_concepts: Writing a generic bad outcome without a feasible interaction sequence.
cards.prompt: Define security misuse case. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A misuse case describes an adversarial or accidental sequence that violates a security objective, including actors, preconditions, path, impact, and candidate controls.

cards.definition: **Definition.** MFA requires evidence from distinct compromise-factor classes and a protocol that binds the factors to the same authentication event.
major_error_concepts: Calling two prompts backed by one shared device secret robust MFA.
cards.prompt: Define multifactor authentication. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: MFA requires evidence from distinct compromise-factor classes and a protocol that binds the factors to the same authentication event.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Network segmentation divides systems into zones with explicit permitted flows and enforcement points to limit reachability and lateral movement.
major_error_concepts: Creating subnets without filtering or identity-aware flow policy and calling them segmented.
cards.prompt: Define network segmentation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Network segmentation divides systems into zones with explicit permitted flows and enforcement points to limit reachability and lateral movement.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A nonce is a value required to be unique or unpredictable according to the protocol and primitive, preventing replay or keystream reuse under its security conditions.
major_error_concepts: Treating nonce reuse as harmless because the nonce is public.
cards.prompt: Define cryptographic nonce. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A nonce is a value required to be unique or unpredictable according to the protocol and primitive, preventing replay or keystream reuse under its security conditions.

cards.definition: **Definition.** OAuth 2.0 delegates bounded resource access among resource owner, client, authorization server, and resource server through defined grants and access tokens.
major_error_concepts: Treating OAuth access-token issuance as user authentication or assuming every token has the same format and audience.
cards.prompt: Define OAuth 2.0 authorization framework. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: OAuth 2.0 delegates bounded resource access among resource owner, client, authorization server, and resource server through defined grants and access tokens.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Contextual output encoding transforms untrusted text so it remains data in one explicitly named textual parser context, such as HTML, JavaScript, CSS, or a URL component; structured query binding and process argument arrays are separate construction mechanisms.
major_error_concepts: Applying one generic escaping function across different parsing contexts.
cards.prompt: Define contextual output encoding. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Contextual output encoding transforms untrusted text so it remains data in one explicitly named textual parser context, such as HTML, JavaScript, CSS, or a URL component; structured query binding and process argument arrays are separate construction mechanisms.

cards.definition: Password hashing stores a per-password salted verifier computed by a purpose-built, configurable-cost password-hashing/KDF scheme to make offline guessing expensive. Memory-hard schemes can strengthen that defense, but not every acceptable scheme exposes a memory-hard work factor: appropriately configured PBKDF2 is a context-dependent example. A salt is not secret and does not replace an adequate work factor; a fast unsalted general-purpose digest is not adequate password storage.
major_error_concepts: Rejecting every properly configured PBKDF2 verifier solely because it is not memory-hard.
Treating a single fast unsalted SHA digest as adequate password storage.
cards.prompt: Define password hashing. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Use a per-password salt and deliberately expensive, configurable password-hashing/KDF computation to resist offline guessing.
Memory hardness is valuable but not a universal definition requirement; salts and cost parameters serve different roles.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Patch management inventories affected assets, prioritizes by exploitability and impact, tests compatibility, deploys, verifies coverage, and handles rollback and exceptions.
major_error_concepts: Marking a vulnerability remediated when a patch exists but is not deployed and verified.
cards.prompt: Define security patch management. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Patch management inventories affected assets, prioritizes by exploitability and impact, tests compatibility, deploys, verifies coverage, and handles rollback and exceptions.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Path traversal manipulates path components, encodings, links, or mount semantics to access resources outside an intended directory boundary.
major_error_concepts: Removing literal ../ once and assuming canonical path containment.
cards.prompt: Define path traversal. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Path traversal manipulates path components, encodings, links, or mount semantics to access resources outside an intended directory boundary.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A penetration test is an authorized, scoped adversarial assessment that attempts to exploit selected attack paths and reports evidence, impact, limitations, and remediation.
major_error_concepts: Calling an automated vulnerability scan a complete penetration test.
cards.prompt: Define penetration test. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A penetration test is an authorized, scoped adversarial assessment that attempts to exploit selected attack paths and reports evidence, impact, limitations, and remediation.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Preimage resistance is the computational property that, given a target digest, an adversary cannot feasibly find an input hashing to that digest under the declared input distribution and attack model.
major_error_concepts: Using collision resistance as though it automatically stated the same adversarial problem as preimage resistance.
cards.prompt: Define preimage resistance. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Preimage resistance is the computational property that, given a target digest, an adversary cannot feasibly find an input hashing to that digest under the declared input distribution and attack model.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A protection domain is a set of code, data, resources, and privileges sharing an enforcement context, such as a process, user, VM, container, or capability domain.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every software module is a protection domain without hardware or reference-monitor enforcement.
cards.prompt: Define protection domain. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A protection domain is a set of code, data, resources, and privileges sharing an enforcement context, such as a process, user, VM, container, or capability domain.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Security mechanisms should make the secure path understandable and usable so users are not systematically pushed toward bypasses.
major_error_concepts: Treating usability as outside the security model.
cards.prompt: Define psychological acceptability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Security mechanisms should make the secure path understandable and usable so users are not systematically pushed toward bypasses.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Security rate limiting bounds operations by principal, resource, time window, cost, and failure state to reduce abuse while considering distributed evasion and denial of service.
major_error_concepts: Applying one global limit that lets one attacker deny service to everyone.
cards.prompt: Define security rate limiting. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Security rate limiting bounds operations by principal, resource, time window, cost, and failure state to reduce abuse while considering distributed evasion and denial of service.

cards.definition: **Role and limitations.** The requirements define the trusted enforcement boundary and explain why bypass resistance, protected execution, and analyzability are jointly needed for access-control assurance. These requirements support assurance only when their implementation is demonstrated; a label alone is not a proof.
major_error_concepts: Relying on a large unreviewed application as the sole enforcement point without identifying its trusted computing base.
cards.prompt: What is reference monitor requirements used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: The requirements define the trusted enforcement boundary and explain why bypass resistance, protected execution, and analyzability are jointly needed for access-control assurance.

cards.definition: **Design principle.** A reference monitor mediates all security-relevant accesses, is tamper resistant, and is small or structured enough to analyze and test.
major_error_concepts: Calling any logging proxy a reference monitor when accesses can bypass it or modify it.
cards.prompt: State the reference-monitor requirements and their intended scope.
required_concepts: A reference monitor mediates all security-relevant accesses, is tamper resistant, and is small or structured enough to analyze and test.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Residual risk is the likelihood and impact remaining after controls, including uncertainty, excluded threats, common-mode failures, and response limitations.
major_error_concepts: Calling risk zero because all planned controls were implemented.
cards.prompt: Define residual security risk. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Residual risk is the likelihood and impact remaining after controls, including uncertainty, excluded threats, common-mode failures, and response limitations.

cards.definition: **Definition.** RBAC assigns permissions to roles and users or services to roles, enabling organizational grouping and separation of duties.
major_error_concepts: Creating one broad administrator role and calling the system least privilege.
cards.prompt: Define role-based access control. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: RBAC assigns permissions to roles and users or services to roles, enabling organizational grouping and separation of duties.

cards.definition: **Role and limitations.** The principles are design lenses for locating excessive trust, hidden bypasses, unusable controls, and shared failure modes; they are not a proof that a system is secure.
major_error_concepts: Treating a checklist of principle names as a completed threat model.
cards.prompt: What are the Saltzer and Schroeder design principles used for, and what is their main limitation?
required_concepts: The principles are design lenses for locating excessive trust, hidden bypasses, unusable controls, and shared failure modes; they are not a proof that a system is secure.
cards.term: Saltzer and Schroeder design principles: role

cards.definition: **Design principle.** The classic principles include economy of mechanism, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, open design, separation of privilege, least privilege, least common mechanism, and psychological acceptability.
major_error_concepts: Using secrecy of design as a substitute for protected keys and reviewable mechanisms.
cards.prompt: State the Saltzer and Schroeder design principles and their scope.
required_concepts: The classic principles include economy of mechanism, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, open design, separation of privilege, least privilege, least common mechanism, and psychological acceptability.
cards.term: Saltzer and Schroeder design principles: statement

cards.definition: **Definition.** The browser same-origin policy restricts how documents or scripts from one origin interact with resources from another, with explicit mechanisms such as CORS relaxing selected reads.
major_error_concepts: Treating same-origin policy as preventing requests from being sent cross-origin.
cards.prompt: Define same-origin policy. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The browser same-origin policy restricts how documents or scripts from one origin interact with resources from another, with explicit mechanisms such as CORS relaxing selected reads.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A sandbox escape exploits an enforcement flaw, exposed authority, shared kernel, helper service, or misconfiguration to act outside the sandbox policy.
major_error_concepts: Calling allowed network access an escape when it was within the stated policy.
cards.prompt: Define sandbox escape. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A sandbox escape exploits an enforcement flaw, exposed authority, shared kernel, helper service, or misconfiguration to act outside the sandbox policy.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A sandbox restricts code to a defined set of resources and operations through enforceable isolation, syscall, filesystem, network, identity, and resource controls.
major_error_concepts: Calling a working directory or prompt instruction a sandbox.
cards.prompt: Define security sandbox. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A sandbox restricts code to a defined set of resources and operations through enforceable isolation, syscall, filesystem, network, identity, and resource controls.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Secret management controls creation, storage, distribution, access, rotation, revocation, audit, and emergency recovery of credentials and keys.
major_error_concepts: Moving secrets from code into an unprotected environment file and calling the lifecycle solved.
cards.prompt: Define secret management. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Secret management controls creation, storage, distribution, access, rotation, revocation, audit, and emergency recovery of credentials and keys.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A secure channel authenticates intended endpoints and protects record confidentiality and integrity, with downgrade, replay, key compromise, and metadata limits stated.
major_error_concepts: Calling encrypted transport secure without verifying endpoint identity.
cards.prompt: Define secure channel. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A secure channel authenticates intended endpoints and protects record confidentiality and integrity, with downgrade, replay, key compromise, and metadata limits stated.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A secure development lifecycle integrates requirements, threat modeling, design review, implementation controls, testing, provenance, release gates, vulnerability response, and lessons into normal delivery.
major_error_concepts: Adding a penetration test at release and calling the lifecycle secure.
cards.prompt: Define secure development lifecycle. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A secure development lifecycle integrates requirements, threat modeling, design review, implementation controls, testing, provenance, release gates, vulnerability response, and lessons into normal delivery.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Security randomness is generated from an approved entropy-seeded CSPRNG and used with domain-appropriate length and uniqueness requirements.
major_error_concepts: Using a reproducible simulation PRNG for session tokens or keys.
cards.prompt: Define cryptographically secure randomness. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Security randomness is generated from an approved entropy-seeded CSPRNG and used with domain-appropriate length and uniqueness requirements.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A security architecture review evaluates assets, flows, trust boundaries, identity, authority, secrets, isolation, dependencies, failure modes, and control placement before implementation is fixed.
major_error_concepts: Reviewing code style without the system's trust and data-flow architecture.
cards.prompt: Define security architecture review. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A security architecture review evaluates assets, flows, trust boundaries, identity, authority, secrets, isolation, dependencies, failure modes, and control placement before implementation is fixed.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A security asset is information, capability, service, identity, money, safety property, reputation, or other value that a system must protect for named stakeholders.
major_error_concepts: Listing infrastructure components without identifying what value their compromise harms.
cards.prompt: Define security asset. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A security asset is information, capability, service, identity, money, safety property, reputation, or other value that a system must protect for named stakeholders.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A detection maps events and context to a hypothesis of malicious or policy-violating behavior with a threshold, evidence, and response path.
major_error_concepts: Calling any anomaly malicious without a threat-linked hypothesis.
cards.prompt: Define security detection. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A detection maps events and context to a hypothesis of malicious or policy-violating behavior with a threshold, evidence, and response path.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A security event is an observable occurrence relevant to a security policy or threat, such as authentication failure, privilege change, sensitive access, or control alert.
major_error_concepts: Treating every log line as a security event of equal importance.
cards.prompt: Define security event. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A security event is an observable occurrence relevant to a security policy or threat, such as authentication failure, privilege change, sensitive access, or control alert.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A security mechanism is a technical or procedural means that enforces, detects, or recovers from violations of a security policy.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a mechanism is effective without mapping it to a policy and threat.
cards.prompt: Define security mechanism. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A security mechanism is a technical or procedural means that enforces, detects, or recovers from violations of a security policy.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A security policy states which principals may perform which operations on which resources under what conditions, independent of the mechanism enforcing it.
major_error_concepts: Treating current implementation behavior as the policy without a normative rule.
cards.prompt: Define security policy. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A security policy states which principals may perform which operations on which resources under what conditions, independent of the mechanism enforcing it.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A principal is an entity that can be authenticated and granted authority, such as a person, service, process, device, or delegated role.
major_error_concepts: Equating a principal with one human username when services and processes also act.
cards.prompt: Define security principal. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A principal is an entity that can be authenticated and granted authority, such as a person, service, process, device, or delegated role.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A security requirement is a testable statement about protected assets, authorized behavior, threat conditions, control behavior, failure state, and evidence.
major_error_concepts: Writing secure as a nonverifiable quality adjective.
cards.prompt: Define security requirement. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A security requirement is a testable statement about protected assets, authorized behavior, threat conditions, control behavior, failure state, and evidence.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A security-test oracle classifies observed executions using crashes, sanitizer findings, invariant violations, policy breaches, unauthorized effects, hangs, or differential behavior while stating detection gaps.
major_error_concepts: Treating absence of a crash as evidence that a fuzzed execution is secure.
cards.prompt: Define security-test oracle. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A security-test oracle classifies observed executions using crashes, sanitizer findings, invariant violations, policy breaches, unauthorized effects, hangs, or differential behavior while stating detection gaps.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Separation of privilege requires multiple independent conditions, roles, or approvals before a sensitive operation is authorized.
major_error_concepts: Splitting one credential into two fields controlled by the same compromised principal.
cards.prompt: Define separation of privilege. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Separation of privilege requires multiple independent conditions, roles, or approvals before a sensitive operation is authorized.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A session carries authenticated context across requests using a protected identifier or token with scope, expiration, renewal, revocation, and binding semantics.
major_error_concepts: Treating possession of a never-expiring bearer token as continuing proof of user presence.
cards.prompt: Define authenticated session. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A session carries authenticated context across requests using a protected identifier or token with scope, expiration, renewal, revocation, and binding semantics.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Shell-safe argument-vector construction invokes a program with an explicit executable and argument array through a non-shell API whenever shell grammar is unnecessary, keeping untrusted values out of command parsing.
major_error_concepts: Joining untrusted values into one shell command string and relying on generic escaping.
cards.prompt: Define shell argument-vector construction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Shell-safe argument-vector construction invokes a program with an explicit executable and argument array through a non-shell API whenever shell grammar is unnecessary, keeping untrusted values out of command parsing.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Signature verification checks a signature against the exact message representation, algorithm parameters, public key, and validation policy and returns a bounded validity result rather than reconstructing the signer.
major_error_concepts: Verifying different canonicalized bytes from those signed or accepting a key without validating its owner and permitted use.
cards.prompt: Define digital-signature verification. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Signature verification checks a signature against the exact message representation, algorithm parameters, public key, and validation policy and returns a bounded validity result rather than reconstructing the signer.

cards.definition: **Definition.** An SBOM records software components, versions, suppliers, and dependency relationships for provenance and vulnerability response.
major_error_concepts: Treating an SBOM as evidence that listed components are trustworthy or vulnerability free.
cards.prompt: Define software bill of materials. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: An SBOM records software components, versions, suppliers, and dependency relationships for provenance and vulnerability response.

cards.definition: **Definition.** SSRF induces a server to make attacker-influenced requests, potentially reaching internal networks, metadata services, or privileged protocols through the server's authority.
major_error_concepts: Blocking one hostname string without accounting for redirects, DNS changes, encodings, and alternate address forms.
cards.prompt: Define server-side request forgery. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: SSRF induces a server to make attacker-influenced requests, potentially reaching internal networks, metadata services, or privileged protocols through the server's authority.

cards.definition: **Definition.** SAST analyzes source or compiled artifacts without executing the deployed program to find patterns, data flows, and weakness candidates.
major_error_concepts: Treating every static warning as an exploitable vulnerability.
cards.prompt: Define static application security testing. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: SAST analyzes source or compiled artifacts without executing the deployed program to find patterns, data flows, and weakness candidates.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Structured parameter binding sends query structure separately from untrusted data through a typed database or API interface so data is not reparsed as query syntax.
major_error_concepts: Escaping data into a query string and calling it equivalent to parameter binding in every grammar.
cards.prompt: Define structured parameter binding. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Structured parameter binding sends query structure separately from untrusted data through a typed database or API interface so data is not reparsed as query syntax.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Symmetric cryptography uses shared secret keying material, while public-key cryptography separates public and private operations; the distinction changes distribution, authentication, compromise, performance, and trust assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming public-key cryptography removes the need to authenticate public keys or protect private keys.
cards.prompt: Distinguish symmetric versus public-key cryptography.
required_concepts: Symmetric cryptography uses shared secret keying material, while public-key cryptography separates public and private operations; the distinction changes distribution, authentication, compromise, performance, and trust assumptions.

cards.definition: A tamper-evident log lets a verifier detect specified alteration, deletion, insertion or reordering attempts under a stated threat model. Mechanisms can include authenticated chaining, signatures, append-only protected storage, or independently retained checkpoints and copies. Access control restricts who can write but alone does not prove alteration would be detectable. A hash chain controlled entirely by the same attacker can be recomputed or truncated unless trusted verification anchors and an appropriate observation protocol expose that change.
major_error_concepts: Calling an editable database table tamper-evident merely because ordinary users lack update permission.
Claiming a wholly rewritable unanchored hash chain detects every complete-history rewrite.
cards.prompt: Define tamper-evident log. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: State what modifications become detectable and the protected mechanism/verification assumptions.
Distinguish restricting writes from detecting tampering, and protect verification evidence against the stated adversary.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A threat model ties assets and objectives to system boundaries, adversaries, trust assumptions, attack paths, controls, residual risks, and explicitly excluded threats.
major_error_concepts: Producing a diagram without adversary capabilities, control claims, and residual risk.
cards.prompt: Define threat model. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A threat model ties assets and objectives to system boundaries, adversaries, trust assumptions, attack paths, controls, residual risks, and explicitly excluded threats.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A threat is a potential adverse event in which an actor or condition exploits a weakness to harm an asset or security objective.
major_error_concepts: Using threat, vulnerability, and realized incident as synonyms.
cards.prompt: Define security threat. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A threat is a potential adverse event in which an actor or condition exploits a weakness to harm an asset or security objective.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A trust boundary is an interface where data, code, identity, or authority crosses between components governed by different assumptions or control domains.
major_error_concepts: Marking only network boundaries while ignoring process, tenant, privilege, and organizational boundaries.
cards.prompt: Define trust boundary. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A trust boundary is an interface where data, code, identity, or authority crosses between components governed by different assumptions or control domains.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The TCB is the collection of hardware, software, and procedures whose correct operation is necessary to enforce the security policy.
major_error_concepts: Calling only the authentication service trusted while ignoring kernels, key stores, policy engines, and update paths.
cards.prompt: Define trusted computing base. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The TCB is the collection of hardware, software, and procedures whose correct operation is necessary to enforce the security policy.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Use-after-free accesses memory after its lifetime ends, allowing stale references to observe or corrupt reallocated objects.
major_error_concepts: Treating a memory leak as use-after-free.
cards.prompt: Define use-after-free. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Use-after-free accesses memory after its lifetime ends, allowing stale references to observe or corrupt reallocated objects.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Coordinated disclosure provides a protected reporting path, triage, validation, remediation timeline, communication, credit, and escalation process for security findings.
major_error_concepts: Publishing exploit details immediately without considering active risk, vendor contact, and user mitigation.
cards.prompt: Define coordinated vulnerability disclosure. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Coordinated disclosure provides a protected reporting path, triage, validation, remediation timeline, communication, credit, and escalation process for security findings.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A vulnerability is a weakness in design, implementation, configuration, operation, or process that can be exploited to violate a security objective.
major_error_concepts: Calling every bug a security vulnerability without a plausible security consequence and path.
cards.prompt: Define security vulnerability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A vulnerability is a weakness in design, implementation, configuration, operation, or process that can be exploited to violate a security objective.

deck.description: Reason about threats, trust boundaries, authentication, authorization, cryptography, secure design, software and network attacks, privacy, and assurance evidence.
deck.subject: Computer Science and Software
deck.title: Security Engineering I
